title: The Alpha Trap
summary: Students maximise Cronbach's alpha by choosing items from a simulated bank, discover that the cheapest route is to ask the same question five ways, and then see the narrow scale they have built fail against a simulated outcome.
learningObjectives: Explain why Cronbach's alpha rises with both the number of items and their average intercorrelation, and why neither is a property of the construct.
Explain why a high alpha is not evidence of unidimensionality.
Explain why a high alpha is not evidence of validity, using the bloated specific factor as the mechanism.
Judge a scale on content coverage and item redundancy rather than on its reliability coefficient alone.
Recognise that a very high alpha in a short scale is a warning about item redundancy rather than a mark of quality.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout using native checkboxes, radios and buttons; the coverage chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible data table carrying the same numbers; state changes announced through the shell's polite live region; redundancy and outcome verdicts state their tone in words as well as by border colour; stage progress carried by aria-current and visible text; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Reliability: why a high Cronbach's alpha is not validity, unidimensionality or evidence of a good measure
itemSource: All 24 items were written for this tool. No published or commercial questionnaire is reproduced, in whole or in part.
simulationNotes: Every figure is the value implied by a fictional correlation model, not an estimate from a sample. Items load on a general factor, a content-area factor and, for near-duplicates, a wording-specific factor; the simulated outcome responds to the general factor and to breadth of coverage but not to wording. No sampling error is modelled, so no confidence intervals are shown. The construct and its five content areas are invented for teaching.
